1 Corinthians.line: Paul writes to the divided church in Corinth, correcting disorders and answering their questions about Christian living and worship.
more: He first confronts factions and calls them back to the message of the cross.
He then addresses sexual immorality, lawsuits, and a case of incest in the church.
He answers their letter on marriage, food offered to idols, and Christian freedom.
He corrects disorder in worship, the Lord's Supper, and the use of spiritual gifts.
He defends the bodily resurrection of Christ and believers, then closes with travel plans and greetings.

1.line: Paul greets the church, thanks God for them, and rebukes their divisions by pointing to the cross.
more: Members were rallying around Paul, Apollos, Cephas, or Christ, splitting the church.
The message of a crucified Christ looks foolish to the world but is God's power and wisdom.
God chose the lowly so that no one could boast except in the Lord.

2.line: Paul explains that he preached Christ crucified simply, so their faith would rest on God's power, not human wisdom.
more: He came in weakness rather than with impressive speech.
God's hidden wisdom is revealed by the Spirit to those who are spiritual.
The natural person cannot accept the things of God's Spirit.

3.line: Paul shows that factions reveal immaturity, since he and Apollos are only servants and God gives the growth.
more: He could only feed them milk because of their jealousy and strife.
Christ is the one foundation, and each builder's work will be tested by fire.
The church is God's temple, and God's Spirit dwells among them.

4.line: Paul describes apostles as servants accountable to God and contrasts his hardships with the Corinthians' pride.
more: He refuses to be judged by human standards before the Lord comes.
The apostles suffer hunger, insult, and persecution, while the Corinthians act as if already reigning.
As their spiritual father, he urges them to imitate him and sends Timothy.

5.line: Paul orders the church to remove a man living in sexual immorality with his father's wife.
more: The church had tolerated the sin rather than mourning over it.
A little leaven spreads through the whole lump, so the old leaven must be cleared out.
Believers must judge immorality within the church, while God judges those outside.

6.line: Paul rebukes believers for suing one another before unbelievers and warns against sexual immorality.
more: It is better to be wronged than to defraud a brother in court.
The unrighteous will not inherit God's kingdom, but the Corinthians have been washed and justified.
Their bodies belong to the Lord and are temples of the Holy Spirit.

7.line: Paul answers questions about marriage, singleness, and divorce, giving guidance for different situations.
more: Husbands and wives owe each other marital rights and should not separate.
A believer married to an unbeliever should not leave if the spouse is willing to stay.
Each should generally remain in the condition in which God called him.
Singleness allows undivided devotion to the Lord, though marriage is no sin.

8.line: Paul addresses food offered to idols, teaching that love must limit the use of knowledge.
more: Idols are nothing, for there is one God and one Lord, Jesus Christ.
Not everyone knows this, and some consciences are weak.
Paul would rather never eat meat than cause a brother to stumble.

9.line: Paul points to his own example of giving up his rights as an apostle for the sake of the gospel.
more: He has the right to financial support but has not used it.
He has become all things to all people to win some.
Like an athlete, he disciplines himself so he will not be disqualified.

10.line: Paul warns from Israel's history against idolatry and tells believers to do everything for God's glory.
more: Israel shared God's blessings in the wilderness yet fell through idolatry and immorality.
God provides a way of escape in every temptation.
Sharing the Lord's table excludes sharing in feasts offered to demons.
Believers should seek others' good and avoid giving offense.

11.line: Paul addresses head coverings in worship and rebukes abuses of the Lord's Supper.
more: He appeals to creation order and custom regarding men and women praying and prophesying.
At the Supper, some ate selfishly while others went hungry.
He repeats the Lord's words instituting the Supper and calls for self-examination.

12.line: Paul teaches that spiritual gifts come from one Spirit and serve one body with many members.
more: No one speaking by the Spirit calls Jesus accursed.
The Spirit distributes different gifts to each person for the common good.
Every member of the body is needed, and all should care for one another.

13.line: Paul shows that love is essential, since even the greatest gifts without love are worthless.
more: Love is patient, kind, and free from envy, pride, and resentment.
Prophecy, tongues, and knowledge will pass away, but love never ends.
Faith, hope, and love remain, and the greatest is love.

14.line: Paul directs that gifts in worship build up the church, favoring prophecy over uninterpreted tongues.
more: Tongues without interpretation do not edify others or outsiders.
Speakers should take turns, with interpretation and evaluation.
He gives instructions about women and orderly conduct in the assemblies.
All things should be done decently and in order.

15.line: Paul defends the resurrection of Christ and explains the future bodily resurrection of believers.
more: Christ died, was buried, rose, and appeared to many witnesses, including Paul.
If Christ is not raised, faith is futile and believers are still in their sins.
The resurrection body will be imperishable, spiritual, and glorious.
At the last trumpet the dead will be raised and death defeated.

16.line: Paul gives instructions for the collection for Jerusalem, shares travel plans, and closes with greetings.
more: Each should set money aside on the first day of every week.
He plans to visit after staying in Ephesus until Pentecost.
He commends Timothy, Apollos, Stephanas, and others, and urges them to do everything in love.

2 Corinthians.line: Paul defends his apostolic ministry to the Corinthians, explaining its sufferings and glory and preparing them for his coming visit.
more: He explains his changed travel plans and his joy at their repentance.
He describes the new covenant ministry as glorious yet carried out in weakness.
He urges reconciliation with God and with himself.
He encourages generous giving to the collection for Jerusalem's believers.
He answers false apostles, boasting reluctantly in his weaknesses before his third visit.

1.line: Paul praises God for comfort in affliction and explains why he changed his plans to visit Corinth.
more: God comforts believers so they can comfort others.
In Asia he despaired of life, learning to rely on God who raises the dead.
He delayed his visit to spare them, not out of fickleness.

2.line: Paul explains his earlier painful letter and urges the church to forgive an offender who has repented.
more: He wrote with many tears, out of love for them.
Forgiveness keeps Satan from gaining an advantage.
God leads his ministers in triumph, spreading the fragrance of Christ.

3.line: Paul contrasts the fading glory of the old covenant with the greater, lasting glory of the Spirit's new covenant.
more: The Corinthians themselves are his letter of recommendation, written by the Spirit.
A veil remains over hearts when the old covenant is read, removed only in Christ.
Believers are being transformed into the Lord's image.

4.line: Paul explains that the gospel's treasure is held in fragile human vessels so the power is clearly God's.
more: He refuses deceptive methods and proclaims Jesus Christ as Lord.
He is afflicted, perplexed, and persecuted, yet not crushed or destroyed.
Present troubles are light compared with eternal glory.

5.line: Paul speaks of the hope of a heavenly body and the ministry of reconciliation entrusted to him.
more: The Spirit is a guarantee of the life to come.
All must appear before the judgment seat of Christ.
In Christ God reconciled the world to himself, and anyone in Christ is a new creation.

6.line: Paul appeals to the Corinthians not to receive God's grace in vain and to avoid unbelieving partnerships.
more: He lists hardships and virtues that commend his ministry.
He asks them to open their hearts to him as he has to them.
Believers are God's temple and must not be yoked with unbelievers.

7.line: Paul rejoices that Titus brought news of the Corinthians' godly grief and repentance.
more: He calls them to cleanse themselves from every defilement.
Godly grief produces repentance, while worldly grief produces death.
Titus's report renewed Paul's confidence in them.

8.line: Paul urges the Corinthians to complete their gift for the Jerusalem believers, following the Macedonians' example.
more: The poor Macedonian churches gave generously beyond their means.
Christ became poor so that they might become rich.
Titus and two trusted brothers will handle the collection with integrity.

9.line: Paul encourages cheerful, generous giving and explains how it results in thanksgiving to God.
more: He wants their gift ready before he arrives so it is not forced.
Whoever sows generously will reap generously, and God loves a cheerful giver.
Their giving meets needs and leads others to glorify God.

10.line: Paul answers critics who say he is bold in letters but weak in person.
more: His weapons are spiritual and destroy arguments raised against the knowledge of God.
He will act in person as he writes in his letters.
He boasts only within the sphere God assigned, seeking the Lord's commendation.

11.line: Paul reluctantly boasts to expose false apostles who preach another Jesus and exploit the Corinthians.
more: He fears they are being led astray as Eve was deceived.
He preached to them free of charge.
False apostles disguise themselves as servants of righteousness.
He lists his labors, imprisonments, beatings, shipwrecks, and anxiety for the churches.

12.line: Paul describes a heavenly vision and a thorn in the flesh, learning that God's power is perfected in weakness.
more: He was caught up to paradise and heard things that cannot be told.
The Lord refused to remove the thorn, saying his grace is sufficient.
He plans a third visit and fears finding unrepentant sin.

13.line: Paul warns that he will not spare unrepentant sinners on his third visit and urges self-examination.
more: Christ was crucified in weakness but lives by God's power.
They should test themselves to see whether they are in the faith.
He closes with appeals for restoration and peace and a blessing in the name of Father, Son, and Spirit.

Galatians.line: Paul defends the gospel of justification by faith in Christ against teachers requiring Gentile believers to keep the law.
more: He insists there is no other gospel and defends his apostleship as received from Christ.
He recounts confronting Peter over separating from Gentile believers.
He argues from Abraham and the law that blessing comes through faith, not works.
He calls believers to stand in freedom and walk by the Spirit.
He closes by boasting only in the cross and the new creation.

1.line: Paul condemns turning to a different gospel and shows his gospel came by revelation from Jesus Christ.
more: Anyone preaching another gospel is accursed, even an angel from heaven.
He once persecuted the church but was called by God's grace.
He did not receive his gospel from the Jerusalem apostles.

2.line: Paul recounts the Jerusalem leaders' approval of his gospel and his rebuke of Peter at Antioch.
more: Titus, a Greek, was not compelled to be circumcised.
Peter withdrew from eating with Gentiles out of fear, and Paul opposed him publicly.
A person is justified by faith in Christ, not by works of the law.

3.line: Paul argues that the Galatians received the Spirit by faith and that Abraham's blessing comes through faith.
more: Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness.
Christ redeemed us from the law's curse by becoming a curse.
The law, given later, served as a guardian until Christ came.
All baptized into Christ are one in him and are Abraham's offspring.

4.line: Paul explains that believers are God's adopted children, not slaves, and pleads with the Galatians not to return to bondage.
more: God sent his Son to redeem those under the law and his Spirit into their hearts.
Paul recalls their warm welcome when he first preached to them while ill.
Hagar and Sarah illustrate two covenants, one of slavery and one of freedom.

5.line: Paul urges believers to stand firm in Christ's freedom and live by the Spirit rather than the flesh.
more: Seeking justification through circumcision means being severed from Christ.
Freedom is not license but an opportunity to serve one another in love.
He contrasts the works of the flesh with the fruit of the Spirit.

6.line: Paul gives practical instructions on bearing burdens and doing good, then closes by boasting only in the cross.
more: Those who are spiritual should restore a sinning brother gently.
People reap what they sow, so believers should not grow weary in doing good.
Circumcision counts for nothing, but a new creation is what matters.

Ephesians.line: Paul explains God's plan to unite all things in Christ and calls the church to live out its new identity.
more: He praises God for spiritual blessings and prays for the believers' understanding.
He shows how God saved sinners by grace and united Jews and Gentiles in one body.
He describes his ministry of revealing this mystery and prays for their strength in love.
He urges unity, holiness, and godly relationships in the home and household.
He closes with a call to stand firm in the armor of God.

1.line: Paul praises God for every spiritual blessing in Christ and prays that believers will know God's power.
more: God chose, adopted, and redeemed believers according to his purpose.
Believers are sealed with the Holy Spirit as a guarantee of their inheritance.
God raised Christ and made him head over all things for the church.

2.line: Paul shows that God saved people dead in sin by grace through faith and united Jews and Gentiles in Christ.
more: Salvation is God's gift, not a result of works.
Christ broke down the dividing wall of hostility through the cross.
Believers together form a holy temple with Christ as cornerstone.

3.line: Paul describes the revealed mystery that Gentiles are fellow heirs and prays for believers to know Christ's love.
more: Paul was given grace to preach Christ's unsearchable riches to the Gentiles.
Through the church God's wisdom is made known to heavenly rulers.
He asks that they be strengthened and filled with God's fullness.

4.line: Paul urges believers to walk worthily in unity and to put off the old self and put on the new.
more: There is one body, one Spirit, one Lord, one faith, and one baptism.
Christ gave leaders to equip the saints and build up the body to maturity.
Believers should put away falsehood, anger, theft, and corrupt talk, and be kind and forgiving.

5.line: Paul calls believers to imitate God, walk in love and light, and be filled with the Spirit.
more: Sexual immorality, impurity, and greed must have no place among them.
They should make the best use of time and give thanks always.
Wives submit to husbands, and husbands love their wives as Christ loved the church.

6.line: Paul gives instructions to children, parents, slaves, and masters, then calls believers to put on God's armor.
more: Children obey parents, and fathers must not provoke their children.
Slaves serve as to Christ, and masters must not threaten them.
The struggle is against spiritual forces, requiring truth, righteousness, faith, the word, and prayer.

Philippians.line: Paul, writing from prison, thanks the Philippians for their partnership and urges them to joy, unity, and Christlike humility.
more: He reports that his imprisonment has advanced the gospel.
He calls for humility, pointing to Christ's self-emptying and exaltation.
He commends Timothy and Epaphroditus.
He warns against confidence in the flesh and presses on toward knowing Christ.
He urges peace and contentment and thanks them for their gift.

1.line: Paul thanks God for the Philippians and explains that his imprisonment has advanced the gospel.
more: He is confident God will complete the good work begun in them.
For him to live is Christ and to die is gain.
He urges them to live worthily of the gospel and stand firm together.

2.line: Paul calls for humble unity by pointing to Christ, who emptied himself, died, and was exalted by God.
more: Believers should count others more significant than themselves.
Every knee will bow and confess Jesus Christ as Lord.
They should work out their salvation, shining as lights in the world.
He plans to send Timothy and is sending back Epaphroditus, who nearly died.

3.line: Paul warns against those who trust in circumcision and counts everything as loss compared to knowing Christ.
more: He had impeccable credentials in Judaism but now seeks righteousness from God through faith.
He presses on toward the goal of God's upward call in Christ.
Believers' citizenship is in heaven, from which they await the Savior.

4.line: Paul urges unity, joy, and peace, and thanks the Philippians for their generous gifts.
more: He appeals to Euodia and Syntyche to agree in the Lord.
Prayer with thanksgiving brings God's peace, which guards hearts and minds.
He has learned contentment in every circumstance through Christ who strengthens him.

Colossians.line: Paul affirms the supremacy and sufficiency of Christ against false teaching and describes the new life believers have in him.
more: He thanks God for the Colossians and praises Christ as Creator and Reconciler.
He describes his labor for the church and warns against deceptive philosophy.
He shows that human rules and ascetic practices cannot restrain the flesh.
He calls believers to set their minds on things above and live as new people.
He gives household instructions and closes with personal greetings.

1.line: Paul gives thanks and prays for the Colossians, then exalts Christ as supreme over creation and the church.
more: Believers were transferred from darkness into the kingdom of God's Son.
Christ is the image of God, through whom all things were created.
Through Christ's death God reconciled them, and Paul labors to present everyone mature in Christ.

2.line: Paul warns against human philosophies and rules, since believers have fullness and victory in Christ.
more: The whole fullness of deity dwells bodily in Christ.
God forgave their debts, nailing the record against them to the cross.
Food laws, festivals, angel worship, and ascetic rules are only shadows.

3.line: Paul calls believers raised with Christ to put off sinful practices and put on Christlike virtues.
more: They should set their minds on things above, where Christ is.
They must put away immorality, anger, and lying, and put on compassion and love.
He gives instructions to wives, husbands, children, fathers, and slaves.

4.line: Paul instructs masters, urges prayer and wise conduct toward outsiders, and sends greetings from his coworkers.
more: He asks prayer for an open door to proclaim Christ.
Tychicus and Onesimus will bring news of Paul.
He asks that this letter also be read in Laodicea.

1 Thessalonians.line: Paul encourages a young, persecuted church, commends its faith, and teaches about holy living and the Lord's return.
more: He thanks God for their conversion and faithful example.
He recalls his conduct among them and his longing to see them.
He rejoices at Timothy's good report of their faith.
He urges sexual purity and brotherly love.
He teaches about believers who have died and about the day of the Lord.

1.line: Paul thanks God for the Thessalonians' faith, love, and hope, and for their example to other believers.
more: The gospel came to them in power and in the Holy Spirit.
They received the word with joy despite affliction.
They turned from idols to serve God and wait for his Son from heaven.

2.line: Paul recalls his sincere and gentle ministry among them and their reception of the word despite persecution.
more: He did not use flattery or seek glory from people.
He cared for them like a nursing mother and a father.
He longed to return but was hindered by Satan.

3.line: Paul explains that he sent Timothy to strengthen them and rejoices at the good news of their faith.
more: He feared that persecution might have unsettled them.
Timothy reported their faith, love, and longing to see Paul.
He prays they will abound in love and be blameless at Christ's coming.

4.line: Paul urges sexual purity and quiet, loving lives, and comforts them about believers who have died.
more: God's will is their sanctification and abstaining from sexual immorality.
Those who have died in Christ will rise first when the Lord descends.
Living believers will be caught up with them to meet the Lord.

5.line: Paul teaches that the day of the Lord will come unexpectedly and gives final exhortations for church life.
more: Believers are children of light and should stay alert and sober.
God has destined them for salvation, not wrath.
They should respect leaders, rejoice, pray, give thanks, and test everything.

2 Thessalonians.line: Paul encourages the persecuted Thessalonians, corrects confusion about the day of the Lord, and warns against idleness.
more: He assures them that God will justly repay their persecutors when Christ returns.
He explains that the day of the Lord has not come and that a rebellion must come first.
He commands them to avoid idleness and to work for their own living.

1.line: Paul commends the Thessalonians' endurance in persecution and assures them of God's justice at Christ's return.
more: Their faith and love are growing despite affliction.
The Lord Jesus will be revealed from heaven with his angels in flaming fire.
Paul prays that God will make them worthy of his calling.

2.line: Paul corrects the claim that the day of the Lord has come, explaining what must happen first.
more: The rebellion must come and the man of lawlessness be revealed.
Something now restrains him, and the Lord Jesus will destroy him at his coming.
Paul thanks God for choosing them and urges them to hold to the traditions he taught.

3.line: Paul asks for prayer and commands the church to deal with idle members who refuse to work.
more: He asks prayer that the word spread and that he be delivered from wicked men.
He worked night and day to set them an example.
Anyone unwilling to work should not eat, and the disobedient should be warned as brothers.

1 Timothy.line: Paul instructs Timothy on guarding sound doctrine and ordering the life and leadership of the church in Ephesus.
more: He charges Timothy to oppose false teachers and recalls the mercy shown to Paul.
He gives instructions about prayer, worship, and qualifications for overseers and deacons.
He warns of departures from the faith and urges Timothy's personal godliness.
He addresses the care of widows, the honor of elders, and the conduct of slaves.
He warns against the love of money and urges Timothy to fight the good fight.

1.line: Paul charges Timothy to confront false teachers and recalls how Christ showed him mercy as the foremost sinner.
more: Some were devoted to myths and endless genealogies.
The law is good when used lawfully against sin.
Hymenaeus and Alexander have made shipwreck of their faith.

2.line: Paul gives instructions for prayer and for the conduct of men and women in public worship.
more: Prayers should be made for all people, including kings and those in authority.
There is one mediator between God and men, Christ Jesus.
Women should dress modestly, and Paul does not permit them to teach or exercise authority over men.

3.line: Paul lists the qualifications for overseers and deacons and explains why he is writing.
more: Overseers must be above reproach, able to teach, and manage their households well.
Deacons must be dignified, tested, and faithful.
The church is the pillar and buttress of the truth, and Paul recites the mystery of godliness.

4.line: Paul warns that some will depart from the faith and urges Timothy to train himself in godliness.
more: False teachers will forbid marriage and require abstaining from foods God created.
Godliness has value for this life and the life to come.
Timothy should set an example and devote himself to Scripture, teaching, and his gift.

5.line: Paul gives instructions on caring for widows and on honoring, correcting, and appointing elders.
more: Families should support their own widows, and the church should help those truly alone.
Elders who rule well are worthy of double honor.
Charges against elders require two or three witnesses, and none should be appointed hastily.

6.line: Paul instructs slaves, warns against false teachers and love of money, and charges Timothy to remain faithful.
more: Godliness with contentment is great gain.
The love of money is a root of all kinds of evils.
The rich should be generous and hope in God, and Timothy must guard what was entrusted to him.

2 Timothy.line: Paul, imprisoned and near death, urges Timothy to endure suffering, guard the gospel, and faithfully preach the word.
more: He reminds Timothy of his faith and calls him not to be ashamed of the gospel.
He uses images of a soldier, an athlete, and a farmer to urge endurance.
He warns of evil in the last days and points Timothy to Scripture.
He charges Timothy to preach the word and reflects on finishing his own course.

1.line: Paul encourages Timothy to fan into flame God's gift and not be ashamed of the gospel or of Paul's chains.
more: He recalls Timothy's sincere faith, shared by his grandmother Lois and mother Eunice.
God gave a spirit of power, love, and self-control.
Many in Asia deserted Paul, but Onesiphorus refreshed him.

2.line: Paul urges Timothy to endure hardship, teach faithfully, and avoid quarrels and false teaching.
more: He should entrust the teaching to faithful men who can teach others.
He should rightly handle the word of truth.
The Lord's servant must be kind and gently correct opponents.

3.line: Paul warns that difficult times will come and urges Timothy to continue in what he learned from Scripture.
more: People will be lovers of self and money, having a form of godliness without its power.
All who desire to live godly lives in Christ will be persecuted.
All Scripture is breathed out by God and equips the believer for every good work.

4.line: Paul charges Timothy to preach the word and reflects on his approaching death and faithful course.
more: People will turn away from sound teaching to myths.
Paul has finished the race and awaits the crown of righteousness.
He asks Timothy to come quickly and notes that the Lord stood by him.

Titus.line: Paul instructs Titus to appoint elders in Crete and teach sound doctrine that produces good works.
more: He gives qualifications for elders and warns against deceptive teachers.
He tells Titus what to teach various groups so that their conduct adorns the gospel.
He reminds believers of God's saving kindness and urges good works and avoiding divisions.

1.line: Paul tells Titus to appoint qualified elders in every town and silence false teachers in Crete.
more: Elders must be above reproach, self-controlled, and hold firmly to sound teaching.
Many deceivers, especially of the circumcision party, were upsetting whole families.
They profess to know God but deny him by their works.

2.line: Paul tells Titus to teach older and younger believers and slaves to live in ways that honor God's word.
more: Titus himself must model good works and sound teaching.
God's grace trains believers to renounce ungodliness and live self-controlled lives.
Believers wait for the appearing of Jesus Christ, who redeemed them.

3.line: Paul urges believers to be submissive and gentle, grounding good works in God's mercy in salvation.
more: God saved them not by works but through regeneration and renewal by the Spirit.
They should avoid foolish controversies and warn a divisive person twice.
Paul gives travel plans and final greetings.

Philemon.line: Paul appeals to Philemon to receive back his slave Onesimus, now a believer, as a beloved brother.
more: Paul thanks God for Philemon's love and faith.
He appeals on the basis of love rather than command.
He offers to repay anything Onesimus owes and expresses confidence in Philemon's obedience.

1.line: Paul writes from prison asking Philemon to welcome Onesimus, whom Paul led to faith, no longer merely as a slave.
more: Paul commends Philemon for refreshing the hearts of the saints.
Onesimus, once useless, has become useful to both Paul and Philemon.
Paul asks Philemon to charge any debt to him and to prepare a guest room.

Hebrews.line: The writer shows Jesus is superior to angels, Moses, and the old priesthood, urging believers to hold fast.
more: Jesus, God's Son, is greater than the angels and became human to save his people.
He is greater than Moses, and readers are warned not to miss God's rest through unbelief.
He is the great high priest after the order of Melchizedek.
His once-for-all sacrifice establishes a better covenant than the old system.
The writer calls readers to persevering faith, following the example of the faithful.
He closes with exhortations to love, holiness, and faithfulness to leaders.

1.line: God has spoken finally through his Son, who is the radiance of God's glory and superior to the angels.
more: The Son made purification for sins and sat down at God's right hand.
A series of Old Testament quotations shows the Son's superiority.
Angels are ministering spirits sent to serve the heirs of salvation.

2.line: The writer warns not to neglect so great a salvation and explains why the Son became fully human.
more: If the message given through angels was binding, ignoring the Lord's message is more serious.
Jesus was made lower than the angels for a little while to taste death for everyone.
By sharing flesh and blood he broke the devil's power and became a merciful high priest.

3.line: Jesus is worthy of more glory than Moses, and readers are warned not to harden their hearts like Israel.
more: Moses was faithful as a servant in God's house, but Christ as a Son over it.
Israel's unbelief in the wilderness kept them from entering God's rest.
Believers should exhort one another daily so none is hardened by sin.

4.line: The writer urges believers to strive to enter God's rest and to draw near to Jesus, their sympathetic high priest.
more: A Sabbath rest still remains for the people of God.
God's word is living and active, discerning thoughts and intentions.
Jesus was tempted in every way as we are, yet without sin.

5.line: Jesus is a high priest appointed by God after the order of Melchizedek, and the readers are rebuked for immaturity.
more: Every high priest is chosen from among men and appointed by God.
Jesus learned obedience through suffering and became the source of eternal salvation.
The readers ought to be teachers but still need milk.

6.line: The writer urges readers toward maturity, warns against falling away, and assures them of God's sure promise.
more: Those who fall away after tasting God's gifts cannot be restored to repentance.
The writer is confident of better things for his readers.
God confirmed his promise to Abraham with an oath, giving hope as an anchor for the soul.

7.line: The writer explains that Melchizedek's priesthood points to Jesus, whose permanent priesthood surpasses the Levitical one.
more: Abraham gave a tenth to Melchizedek, who blessed him.
A change in the priesthood requires a change in the law.
Jesus lives forever to intercede and offered himself once for all.

8.line: Jesus serves as high priest in the true heavenly sanctuary and mediates a better covenant.
more: The earthly sanctuary is a copy and shadow of the heavenly one.
God promised through Jeremiah a new covenant written on hearts.
The new covenant makes the first one obsolete.

9.line: The writer contrasts the repeated sacrifices of the earthly tabernacle with Christ's once-for-all offering of his own blood.
more: The high priest entered the Most Holy Place once a year with blood.
Christ's blood purifies the conscience and secures eternal redemption.
Christ appeared once to bear sins and will appear a second time to save.

10.line: Christ's single sacrifice perfects believers, so they should draw near to God, hold fast, and not shrink back.
more: The blood of bulls and goats can never take away sins.
Believers should keep meeting together and encourage one another.
Deliberate sin after receiving the truth brings fearful judgment.
They should remember their earlier endurance and live by faith.

11.line: The writer defines faith and lists Old Testament believers who trusted God's promises and acted on them.
more: Faith is the assurance of things hoped for and conviction of things not seen.
Examples include Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Sarah, Moses, and Rahab.
Many suffered and died without receiving what was promised.

12.line: The writer urges readers to run with endurance, looking to Jesus, and to accept God's discipline as his children.
more: God disciplines those he loves for their good.
Believers should pursue peace and holiness and not reject God's grace as Esau did.
They have come not to Mount Sinai but to the heavenly Jerusalem.

13.line: The writer closes with practical exhortations on love, purity, contentment, and following faithful leaders.
more: Believers should show hospitality and remember those in prison.
Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever.
They should offer praise to God and obey their leaders, and the letter ends with a blessing.

James.line: James teaches that genuine faith shows itself in endurance, obedience, controlled speech, humility, and care for others.
more: He addresses trials and temptation and calls readers to be doers of the word.
He condemns favoritism and insists that faith without works is dead.
He warns about the tongue and contrasts earthly and heavenly wisdom.
He rebukes worldliness, pride, and the oppression of the poor by the rich.
He urges patience until the Lord comes and commends the prayer of faith.

1.line: James teaches that trials produce steadfastness and that believers must be doers of the word, not hearers only.
more: Those lacking wisdom should ask God in faith.
Temptation comes from one's own desire, not from God.
Pure religion cares for orphans and widows and remains unstained by the world.

2.line: James condemns favoritism toward the rich and teaches that faith without works is dead.
more: Showing partiality breaks the royal law to love one's neighbor.
Even demons believe and shudder.
Abraham and Rahab showed their faith by their actions.

3.line: James warns about the destructive power of the tongue and contrasts earthly wisdom with wisdom from above.
more: Teachers will be judged with greater strictness.
The tongue is small but, like a spark, can set a forest ablaze.
Wisdom from above is pure, peaceable, gentle, and full of mercy.

4.line: James traces quarrels to selfish desires and calls readers to humble themselves before God.
more: Friendship with the world is enmity with God.
God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.
They should not slander one another or boast about tomorrow.

5.line: James warns rich oppressors, urges patience until the Lord's coming, and teaches about prayer for the sick.
more: Wages withheld from workers testify against the rich.
Believers should be patient like farmers and steadfast like Job.
The prayer of a righteous person is powerful, as Elijah's prayers showed.

1 Peter.line: Peter encourages scattered believers facing suffering to live holy lives, rooted in their living hope in Christ.
more: He praises God for new birth to a living hope and calls readers to holiness.
He describes believers as God's people and urges good conduct among unbelievers.
He instructs on submission to authorities, masters, and spouses, following Christ's example.
He explains how to suffer for doing good as Christ did.
He charges elders to shepherd the flock and urges humility and resistance to the devil.

1.line: Peter praises God for the living hope of salvation and calls believers to be holy as God is holy.
more: Trials test faith, proving it more precious than gold.
The prophets searched into the salvation now announced to them.
They were ransomed by Christ's precious blood and born again through God's word.

2.line: Peter describes believers as living stones and God's chosen people, and urges honorable conduct and submission.
more: Christ is the cornerstone, precious to believers but a stone of stumbling to others.
They should honor rulers and live as free servants of God.
Servants should endure unjust suffering, following Christ, who bore sins on the tree.

3.line: Peter instructs wives and husbands and teaches believers how to respond when suffering for righteousness.
more: Wives may win unbelieving husbands by their conduct, and husbands should honor their wives.
Believers should not repay evil for evil and should be ready to explain their hope.
Christ suffered once for sins to bring people to God.

4.line: Peter calls believers to live for God's will and to rejoice when they share Christ's sufferings.
more: Former pagan practices should be left behind, for the end is near.
They should love earnestly and use their gifts to serve one another.
Suffering as a Christian is no cause for shame.

5.line: Peter exhorts elders to shepherd God's flock willingly and calls all to humility and watchfulness.
more: Elders should lead by example, not for gain or by domineering.
Believers should cast their anxieties on God, who cares for them.
The devil prowls like a lion and must be resisted firmly in the faith.

2 Peter.line: Peter urges believers to grow in godliness and warns against false teachers who deny the Lord's return.
more: He calls readers to add virtues to their faith and affirms the reliability of the apostolic witness.
He describes the character and certain judgment of false teachers.
He explains the apparent delay of the Lord's coming and urges holy living.

1.line: Peter calls believers to grow in godly qualities and grounds their confidence in eyewitness testimony and prophecy.
more: God's power has granted all things needed for life and godliness.
They should add virtue, knowledge, self-control, steadfastness, godliness, affection, and love to their faith.
Peter witnessed Christ's majesty at the transfiguration, and prophecy came from God through the Spirit.

2.line: Peter warns that false teachers will arise and that God will surely judge them as he judged others before.
more: God judged sinning angels, the ancient world, and Sodom and Gomorrah, yet rescued Noah and Lot.
The false teachers are greedy, sensual, and arrogant.
Returning to corruption after knowing Christ leaves them worse off than before.

3.line: Peter answers scoffers who deny Christ's return and urges believers to live holy lives while they wait.
more: With the Lord one day is as a thousand years.
God is patient, not wishing that any should perish.
The day of the Lord will come like a thief, followed by new heavens and a new earth.

1 John.line: John writes so believers may know they have eternal life, shown by obedience, love, and right belief about Jesus.
more: He proclaims the incarnate Word of life and calls readers to walk in the light.
He gives marks of truly knowing God: obedience, love, and confessing Christ.
He warns against antichrists who deny that Jesus is the Christ come in the flesh.
He grounds love for one another in God's love shown in sending his Son.
He closes with assurance of eternal life and confidence in prayer.

1.line: John proclaims the eternal Word of life he witnessed, so readers may share fellowship with God and one another.
more: God is light, and in him is no darkness at all.
Walking in the light brings fellowship and cleansing by Jesus' blood.
If we confess our sins, God is faithful to forgive.

2.line: John teaches that knowing God is shown by keeping his commands and loving others, and warns against antichrists.
more: Jesus Christ is the advocate with the Father and the propitiation for sins.
Believers must not love the world, which is passing away.
Those who deny that Jesus is the Christ are antichrists.

3.line: John explains that God's children do not keep on sinning but practice righteousness and love one another.
more: The Father has lavished love on believers, calling them his children.
Christ appeared to destroy the works of the devil.
Love is shown in deeds, just as Christ laid down his life for us.

4.line: John tells readers to test the spirits and teaches that God is love, so believers must love one another.
more: Every spirit confessing that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God.
God showed his love by sending his Son as the propitiation for sins.
Perfect love casts out fear, and whoever loves God must love his brother.

5.line: John teaches that faith in Jesus overcomes the world and assures believers that they have eternal life.
more: Loving God means keeping his commandments, which are not burdensome.
God has testified that eternal life is in his Son.
Believers can pray with confidence and should keep themselves from idols.

2 John.line: John urges a chosen lady and her children to walk in truth and love and to reject deceivers.
more: John rejoices that some of her children are walking in the truth.
He reminds them of the command to love one another.
He warns against welcoming teachers who deny that Christ came in the flesh.

1.line: The elder commends walking in truth, renews the call to love, and forbids receiving false teachers.
more: Love means walking according to God's commandments.
Many deceivers deny that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh.
John hopes to visit and speak face to face.

3 John.line: John commends Gaius for showing hospitality to traveling missionaries and contrasts him with the domineering Diotrephes.
more: John rejoices that Gaius walks in the truth.
He condemns Diotrephes for rejecting John's authority and refusing to welcome the brothers.
He commends Demetrius and hopes to visit soon.

1.line: The elder praises Gaius's faithfulness, rebukes Diotrephes, and recommends Demetrius.
more: Supporting traveling workers makes believers fellow workers for the truth.
Diotrephes loves to be first and puts those who welcome the brothers out of the church.
John urges Gaius to imitate good, not evil.

Jude.line: Jude urges believers to contend for the faith against ungodly people who have crept into the church.
more: He recalls past examples of God's judgment on unbelief and rebellion.
He describes the false teachers' character and coming judgment.
He calls believers to build themselves up, keep in God's love, and show mercy.
He closes with praise to God, who is able to keep them from stumbling.

1.line: Jude warns against intruders who pervert God's grace into sensuality and calls believers to remain faithful.
more: Israel in the wilderness, rebellious angels, and Sodom illustrate God's judgment.
The intruders are compared to Cain, Balaam, and Korah.
Believers should pray in the Holy Spirit and rescue others.
The letter ends with a doxology to God our Savior.

Revelation.line: John records visions revealing Christ's victory, God's judgment on evil, and the coming new creation where God dwells with his people.
more: John sees the risen Christ, who sends messages to seven churches.
He sees God's heavenly throne and the Lamb who opens a sealed scroll.
Judgments unfold through seals, trumpets, and bowls.
He sees the conflict between the dragon, the beasts, and God's people.
Babylon falls, Christ returns, and Satan and death are defeated.
God makes all things new and dwells with his people.

1.line: John, exiled on Patmos, sees a vision of the glorified Christ standing among seven golden lampstands.
more: The book is a revelation from Jesus Christ, with a blessing for those who read it.
Christ appears with eyes like fire and a voice like many waters.
The lampstands are the seven churches, and the stars are their angels.

2.line: Christ sends messages to the churches in Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, and Thyatira, commending and rebuking them.
more: Ephesus has abandoned the love it had at first.
Smyrna is told to be faithful unto death.
Pergamum and Thyatira tolerate false teaching and immorality.
Each message promises rewards to the one who conquers.

3.line: Christ sends messages to the churches in Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea.
more: Sardis has a reputation for being alive but is dead.
Philadelphia has kept Christ's word and is given an open door.
Laodicea is lukewarm and self-satisfied, and Christ stands at the door and knocks.

4.line: John is taken up to heaven and sees God seated on his throne, surrounded by continual worship.
more: Twenty-four elders sit on thrones around the throne.
Four living creatures cry holy, holy, holy day and night.
The elders worship God as Creator of all things.

5.line: John sees a sealed scroll that only the Lamb, who was slain, is worthy to open.
more: John weeps because no one is found worthy to open the scroll.
The Lion of Judah appears as a Lamb who ransomed people from every nation.
All creation joins in praising God and the Lamb.

6.line: The Lamb opens the first six seals, bringing conquest, war, famine, death, martyrs' cries, and cosmic upheaval.
more: Four horsemen ride out on white, red, black, and pale horses.
The souls of martyrs under the altar ask how long until judgment.
People of every rank hide from the wrath of the Lamb.

7.line: Before further judgment, God's servants are sealed, and a great multitude worships before the throne.
more: One hundred forty-four thousand from the tribes of Israel are sealed.
A countless multitude from every nation stands clothed in white robes.
They have come out of the great tribulation, and God will wipe away every tear.

8.line: The seventh seal is opened, and the first four of seven trumpets bring judgments on the earth.
more: There is silence in heaven for about half an hour.
The prayers of the saints rise with incense before God.
The trumpets strike land, sea, rivers, and heavenly lights, and an eagle announces three woes.

9.line: The fifth and sixth trumpets release demonic locusts and a vast army, yet survivors still refuse to repent.
more: Locusts from the bottomless pit torment those without God's seal.
Four angels bound at the Euphrates are released to kill a third of mankind.
Survivors keep worshiping idols and practicing murder, sorcery, and theft.

10.line: A mighty angel with a little scroll announces that God's mystery will soon be fulfilled.
more: John is told to seal up what the seven thunders said.
He eats the scroll, sweet in his mouth but bitter in his stomach.
He is told to prophesy again about many peoples and nations.

11.line: John measures the temple, two witnesses prophesy and are raised, and the seventh trumpet proclaims Christ's reign.
more: The nations trample the holy city for forty-two months.
The beast kills the two witnesses, but God raises them and takes them to heaven.
Heaven declares that the kingdom of the world has become the Lord's.

12.line: John sees a woman, her child, and a great red dragon, identified as Satan, who wars against God's people.
more: The dragon seeks to devour the woman's child, who is caught up to God.
Michael and his angels defeat the dragon, who is thrown down to earth.
Believers conquer him by the Lamb's blood and their testimony.

13.line: Two beasts arise, one from the sea and one from the earth, empowered by the dragon to deceive and persecute.
more: The sea beast blasphemes God and makes war on the saints.
The earth beast performs signs and makes people worship the first beast.
No one can buy or sell without the beast's mark, whose number is 666.

14.line: The Lamb stands on Mount Zion with the redeemed, and angels announce the gospel, Babylon's fall, and judgment.
more: The 144,000 follow the Lamb wherever he goes.
Those who worship the beast will drink the wine of God's wrath.
The earth is harvested, and the winepress of God's wrath is trodden.

15.line: John sees seven angels with the seven last plagues, while the victorious sing the song of Moses and the Lamb.
more: The conquerors stand beside a sea of glass mingled with fire.
They praise God's just and true ways.
The heavenly temple fills with smoke from God's glory.

16.line: The seven bowls of God's wrath are poured out on the earth, culminating in judgment on Babylon.
more: The bowls bring sores, blood, scorching heat, darkness, and a dried-up Euphrates.
People curse God rather than repent.
Kings are gathered at Armageddon, and the seventh bowl brings a great earthquake.

17.line: John sees Babylon as a prostitute riding a scarlet beast, and an angel explains the vision.
more: She is drunk with the blood of the saints.
The beast's heads and horns represent kings who make war on the Lamb.
The Lamb conquers them, and the beast turns against the prostitute.

18.line: Heaven announces the fall of Babylon, and kings, merchants, and sailors mourn her sudden ruin.
more: God's people are called to come out of her.
Her luxury and trade come to nothing in a single hour.
A millstone thrown into the sea pictures her violent overthrow.

19.line: Heaven rejoices over Babylon's judgment, and Christ rides out as a warrior to defeat the beast and its armies.
more: The marriage supper of the Lamb is announced.
The rider on the white horse is called Faithful and True and the Word of God.
The beast and the false prophet are thrown into the lake of fire.

20.line: Satan is bound for a thousand years, then released, defeated, and cast into the lake of fire before the final judgment.
more: Those who were faithful come to life and reign with Christ for a thousand years.
Satan gathers the nations for battle, but fire from heaven consumes them.
The dead are judged from the books, and death and Hades are thrown into the lake of fire.

21.line: John sees a new heaven and a new earth and the holy city, New Jerusalem, where God dwells with his people.
more: God will wipe away every tear, and death will be no more.
The city shines with God's glory and has gates of pearl and a street of gold.
It needs no temple or sun, for God and the Lamb are its temple and light.

22.line: John sees the river and tree of life, and the book closes with Christ's promise to come soon.
more: God's servants will see his face and reign forever.
John is told not to seal up the words of the prophecy.
Nothing may be added to or taken from the book, which ends praying for Jesus to come.
